title: Working in the 3D model yourself
ask: Do you want to open and change the car's 3D model yourself in a CAD program, or only look at it in the app?
why: If only the agent builds the model, it is written as scripts that rebuild it from the record's numbers with free tools, and you see the result in the app. If you want to change it by hand, it has to live in a program you use, in that program's file format, and the scripts have to work around your edits. The answer picks the tool everything else is built in.
options:
(a) Only look at it in the app. The agent builds it from scripts with free tools (FreeCAD, already on the Mac). Costs nothing and closes off nothing: any part can still be exported as a standard STEP or STL file for a machine shop or a 3D printer.
(b) You also work in it, in FreeCAD. Free, and the files open on the Mac and the Fedora PC. Your hand edits and the agent's scripts have to be kept from overwriting each other, which slows the agent's side.
(c) You also work in it, in a program you name (Fusion 360, Onshape, SolidWorks or another). The model then follows that program's format. Some of these are paid or online-only, and the agent cannot run most of them, so it could only prepare parts for you to assemble.
recommend: (a), unless you want to draw or change parts yourself - then (b)
stops: The proof of the tool chain (A04) and every modelled part after it. The coverage count, the frame and the model's tables (A01-A03) go ahead.

title: How far inside a part the model goes
ask: Should the model stop at each part as it comes off the car in one piece, or also open up units like the engine, gearbox and alternator into their internal parts?
why: The car's parts list has 975 parts. Modelling each one as the single piece that comes off the car, outside shape only, is one size of job. Opening the engine, gearbox, carburettor, alternator, steering box and rear axle into their rotors, gears and bearings is several times that, and those insides can only be measured with each unit apart on a bench. The answer also sets what a service view can show: taking a part off and fitting it, or rebuilding it.
options:
(a) Every part as it comes off the car, outside shape only, with its fasteners. Service views show removal and fitting. The insides of any one unit can be added later without redoing the rest.
(b) As (a), plus the insides of the units you expect to open yourself. Name them in words (for example the carburettor, the brake calipers, the engine). More of your bench time for each unit named.
(c) Everything, down to the insides of every unit. By far the longest road, and until a unit is apart its insides could only come from factory drawings, not from this car.
recommend: (a), unless there is a unit you already know you will rebuild - then (b), naming it
stops: The parts plan (A05): the list of what gets modelled and what you would have to measure.

title: How real measurements get into the model
ask: How do you want to capture the shapes and sizes of the car's parts so the model is true: by hand as parts come off, with a 3D scanner, or with phone photos?
why: The agent cannot see the car. The factory manuals give the body's main dimensions (length, wheelbase, track, the underbody points) but not the shape of most parts, and the free models found online are other people's approximations of similar cars. Without sizes taken from this car the model is a good-looking guess, with every unmeasured size marked unconfirmed. The method decides how much of your time it takes, whether anything is bought, and how true the result is.
options:
(a) By hand: calipers, a tape and photos against a ruler, as each part comes off during the strip and the builds. Nothing to buy. True to about a millimetre on simple parts, weak on curved ones (body panels, the dash, trim). The most of your time.
(b) A handheld 3D scanner. A purchase, not yet priced (a sourcing row prices it if you pick this). Captures curved parts and whole areas such as the engine bay or the bare shell in minutes, and the agent turns the scans into clean parts. The least of your time.
(c) Phone photos: many overlapping pictures of a part, turned into a 3D shape by free software. Nothing to buy. Good for shape, needs a ruler in the picture for size, poor on shiny or black parts.
(d) Nothing measured for now: factory figures and found models only. No effort from you, and the model stays marked unconfirmed everywhere it is not a factory dimension.
recommend: (a), with (c) for the curved parts, unless you are willing to buy a scanner - then (b), which takes far less of your time
stops: Your measuring row (B02) and every part's move from unconfirmed to confirmed. The first pass from factory figures and found models (B01) goes ahead without it.
